column3: Near-verbatim parallel: Ibrahim asks his father and people what they worship.
The prohibition on calling what cannot benefit or harm supplies the functional test developed in the focus passage.
A prophet addresses his people with the exclusive-worship call, but lacks the focus's inherited-idolatry interrogation.
Ibrahim's declaration to his father and people directly answers the allegiance questioned at 26:70.
Immediate answer: they identify idols and their continuing devotional attachment to them.
Exclusive worship of God contrasts with the focus's unnamed objects of worship, though the family setting is absent.
Ibrahim addresses father and people about their devotional attachment to carved images in a close parallel scene.
Immediate continuation tests whether the objects can hear those who call on them.
A father's question about later worship frames inherited religion positively, contrasting the focus's inherited false practice.
Ibrahim asks his father why he worships what cannot hear, see, or benefit, making the focus's question explicit.
It applies the same worship test: the object possesses neither harm nor benefit.
The bare mention of Ibrahim's people does not clarify the question about their worship.
Immediate continuation restates the inquiry and turns their customary worship into an object of examination.
Immediate continuation asks whether the objects can benefit or harm their devotees.
Its rejected route and prophetic-warning context do not clarify inherited worship or its functional test.
Ibrahim and his followers publicly disavow what their people worship, extending the focus's challenge into separation.
The call-and-answer branch is remote from the focus's test of idols and adds no specific worship relation.
Its rejected route concerns a different scene and gives no useful parallel to the focus.
False gods appear in a political threat, but not in Ibrahim's inherited-worship inquiry.
Immediate answer: ancestral custom is offered instead of a reason for the worship under question.
Noah's call to his people for exclusive worship gives a broad prophetic counterpart without the inherited-idol setting.
The account of Pharaoh's destruction does not illuminate the focus's question or its answer.
Ibrahim asks whether they worship what cannot benefit or harm, directly developing the focus's scrutiny.
A mission to a criminal people has no material relation to the object of worship.
Ibrahim's rhetorical question exposes worship of objects the worshippers themselves carve.
Calling on what can neither harm nor benefit closely supplies the focus passage's utility criterion.
The mention of forefathers concerns resurrection disbelief, not inherited worship.
Ibrahim challenges his father and people for taking idols as gods in a closely aligned family-and-community scene.
Immediate continuation expands the ancestral defense to the most distant forebears.
The unguided community context does not clarify the focus's worship question.
A prophet's address to his people and call to reverence broadly parallels the focus's communal challenge.
It identifies worship of what cannot benefit or harm and the human support that sustains the powerless rival.
Withdrawal from people and what they worship shows a practical response to an idolatrous allegiance.
Within the same passage, the question "where are those you worshipped" exposes the objects' final absence.
Immediate continuation identifies the worshipped objects as enemies, except for the Lord of the worlds.
Forefathers are invoked as resurrection evidence, only distantly resembling the focus's ancestral defense.
It groups worshippers with their objects, broadening the relation interrogated in the focus.
Taking desire as a god offers a broader form of misplaced worship, without the family-and-community setting.
The rejected paternal-title reading has no relation to the focus's worship inquiry.
The explicit refusal to worship what others worship marks the same allegiance boundary, though without Ibrahim's inquiry.
Ibrahim rebukes both the people and what they worship besides God, directly continuing the same polemic.
A mission to a criminal people does not clarify the worship relation at issue.
Its father-and-son negotiation has no worship or idolatry connection.
Immediate continuation asks whether the false objects can give aid or defend themselves.
Exclusive worship of God is a broad alternative to the focus's false worship, without its specific scene.
The question about Yusuf's treatment is unrelated to worship or inherited practice.
The denial of mutual power over benefit and harm reinforces the passage's test of alleged divine agency.
Demanding the return of forefathers concerns resurrection proof, not the authority of ancestral worship.
A son's report to his father has no material link to the focus.
Immediate aftermath places the false objects and their followers together in the consequence of their allegiance.
Family flight on the Day of Judgment does not clarify inherited worship.
A prophet's rebuke of sexual wrongdoing is not relevant to the focus's idolatry question.
The supposed patron's harm being nearer than benefit sharpens the utility test applied in the focus passage.
Finding forefathers astray identifies inherited error, though it does not itself test the worshipped objects.
The parallel Lot rebuke concerns a different communal wrongdoing.
Iblis's assembled troops in the immediate punishment scene do not clarify the worship question.
Noah's earlier lawless people provide only a remote communal-consequence backdrop to the focus.
The people explicitly justify their idol worship by saying they found their fathers devoted to it.
God's responsive call contrasts fruitfully with the silent objects interrogated in the focus's continuation.
Musa's relation to his people does not illuminate their object of worship.
Ibrahim's submission to the Lord gives a distant positive alternative, but not the focus's family challenge.
Immediate continuation shows the idolaters disputing after the failure of their allegiance is exposed.
Shuayb's call to his people for worship of God is a broad prophetic counterpart to the focus.
Musa's address to his people lacks a worship-object or inherited-practice connection.
The admission that the idols cannot speak directly supports the focus passage's test of whether they hear.
Ibrahim's station and pilgrimage concern true worship but add little to the interrogated idol cult.
Yusuf asks what they and their fathers worship, calls the objects unauthorized names, and commands worship of God alone.
The challenge to ask the idol if it can speak sets up the same exposure of inert objects.
Continuous remembrance and reflection do not clarify inherited idolatry.
Qarun's conflict with his people has no relevant worship connection.
Its remote branch relation and temptation setting do not clarify the focus scene.
Creation for worship gives the broad positive frame, but not the focus's challenge to false objects.
False partners deny that the people worshipped them, exposing the failed relationship questioned in the focus.
Ibrahim prays that he and his descendants be kept from worshipping idols, extending the family dimension of the focus.
Forefathers occur only in a resurrection objection, not an inherited-worship argument.
Hud's call to his people for exclusive worship broadly parallels the focus's communal address.
Ibrahim says the idols have led many astray, supplying the consequence of the attachment questioned in the focus.
Noah's complaint of rejection does not clarify the idol-worship exchange.
The question about Israel's deviation lacks a direct worship-object connection.
Ibrahim establishes his descendants near the sacred house for prayer, a distant positive worship contrast.
The recognition of unfamiliar visitors has no material relation to the focus.
Leaders reject a new message because they never heard it from forefathers, a general inherited-authority parallel.
Ibrahim's direct call to his people to worship God provides the positive alternative to the focus's question.
Its father-and-daughter setting does not involve worship or inherited religious practice.
Calling a people criminal does not clarify the false-worship relation.
Exclusive worship of God alongside kindness to parents distinguishes divine worship from familial obligation.
The catalogue of earlier deniers adds no specific insight into the focus's question.
Worship expressed through gratitude is a broad positive use of the root without the focus's polemic.
Noah's warning to his people lacks an object-of-worship relation.
The people resist messengers because they would turn them from what their fathers worshipped, directly paralleling inherited allegiance.
The request concerning a brother from their father has no worship connection.
The final mutual exclusion of worship consolidates the allegiance boundary at issue in the focus.
The catalogue of worshipful virtues gives a broad positive ideal but no specific aid to the focus scene.
Its redefinition of paternal relation is not materially connected to inherited worship.
The compressed destruction formula does not clarify the focus.
The appeal to prior messengers asks whether any authorized gods besides the Merciful, a broad historical counterpart.
Treasures and an honored station do not clarify Ibrahim's worship question.
The reference to God's servants is only a broad worship-related term, without the focus's relation.
Its harm-and-benefit language concerns magic and false teaching, not the worship inquiry.
Associating ancestors with idolatry as an excuse parallels the focus's exposure of inherited, unsupported practice.
Ibrahim tells his father that revealed knowledge has reached him and asks him to follow a sound path instead.
Ibrahim directly tells his father not to worship Satan, identifying the deeper allegiance behind false worship.
The father's hostile response shows the family resistance provoked by Ibrahim's challenge to inherited devotion.
Ibrahim explicitly judges both the people and their fathers to be in manifest error, exposing the ancestral premise behind their worship.
Ibrahim announces an intended action against their idols after they turn away, moving from interrogation to confrontation.
The destruction of all but the chief idol stages the examination of the objects' claimed agency.
The people summon Ibrahim and ask whether he acted against their gods, continuing the public inquiry into the cult objects.
The people briefly recognize that they themselves are wrongdoers, the internal verdict elicited by the idol test.
Their decision to burn Ibrahim shows how inherited idol allegiance answers failed argument with coercion.
Ibrahim names the Lord as his Creator and Guide, giving the true functional counterpart to the objects questioned at 26:70.
The Lord's provision of food and drink supplies capacities the idols cannot claim.
Ibrahim identifies the Lord as the one who heals him, extending the passage's test of effective power.
The Lord's power over death and life decisively contrasts with inert worshipped objects.
Ibrahim locates hoped-for forgiveness in the Lord alone, completing the positive allegiance contrast.
The idolaters' final confession calls their prior devotion manifest error.
Their confession specifies the error: they equated false objects with the Lord of the worlds.
They identify misleading criminals as the agents who led them into the false allegiance questioned earlier.
The absence of intercessors exposes the failure of the support they expected from their worship network.
Their wish to return and become believers confirms the irreversible failure of the former worship.
Ibrahim identifies what his people worship besides God as idols and fabricated falsehood, then redirects them to God's provision.
The verse explains that idolatry has become a bond of mutual affection, clarifying the communal attachment behind the focus.
Ibrahim asks the idols why they do not eat and why they do not speak, directly testing their inertness.
The question "what is wrong with you that you do not speak" makes the hearing-and-response failure explicit.
Ibrahim's striking of the idols follows the same practical exposure of their incapacity.
God's creation of both people and what they make overturns worship of humanly fashioned objects.
The Prophet is forbidden to worship those called besides God, establishing the same exclusive allegiance boundary.
The question whether to call on what neither benefits nor harms closely parallels the focus passage's utility test.
The idols create nothing and are themselves created, directly challenging their fitness for worship.
The idols cannot help their worshippers or help themselves, anticipating the questions in 26:72-73 and 26:93.
Those called besides God cannot answer a call, directly matching the focus passage's hearing test.
The alleged partners cannot help their worshippers or help themselves, repeating the failed-support criterion.
People worship what cannot harm or benefit and call the objects intercessors, closely matching the focus's polemic.
The gods called besides God did not avail their people when divine judgment came, giving the consequence of powerless worship.
Those called besides God cannot answer at all, a direct broader parallel to the focus's question about hearing.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, directly denying their divine capacity.
The worshipped objects are dead and unaware, reinforcing the focus passage's test of living response.
People worship what holds no provision from heaven or earth and has no power, a direct functional parallel.
The prohibition on setting up likenesses for God guards against the false equivalence exposed in the focus narrative.
Those called besides God cannot remove harm or transfer it, extending the benefit-and-harm test.
The companions condemn their people's adoption of gods without clear authority, a communal counterpart to Ibrahim's challenge.
People take gods besides God for supposed honor, identifying the expected social function of false worship.
The false gods will deny their worship and become enemies, supplying the final reversal of the focus's allegiance.
The calf is named as a god for worshippers who forget the true divine relation, a direct idol-cult parallel.
Harun warns that the calf is a trial and directs the people back to the Merciful, a close corrective counterpart.
The calf's fate publicly exposes the object that was made into a god.
Only God is declared the true deity, with knowledge encompassing all things, against the made object.
People worship besides God without revealed authority or knowledge, directly rejecting the basis for the focus's inherited practice.
The alleged gods create nothing, are created, and control neither harm nor benefit, life nor death.
God's question about alleged partners on the Day of Judgment tests the objects' availability and reality.
Those for whom punishment is due admit that the worshippers did not truly worship them.
The call to summon partners exposes that they cannot answer or provide guidance.
Associates will provide no intercession, showing the collapse of partnership claims.
The parable rejects assigning partners to God, directly challenging the equivalence assumed in false worship.
Those called besides God possess nothing and have no share or supporting power, a compact statement of their impotence.
The angels ask whether people worshipped them, beginning a formal disavowal of mistaken devotion.
The angels deny the worship and identify the actual allegiance as directed to jinn, exposing the misdescribed cult relation.
Those called besides God do not possess even a fragment of sovereignty.
The objects cannot hear calls and, if they heard, could not answer; on Judgment they deny the association.
Adopting gods besides God is rejected because their intercession cannot help and they cannot save from harm.
People take gods besides God hoping for help, directly naming the expected but failed function of idols.
The false gods cannot help their worshippers even as the worshippers stand mobilized in their service.
The worshippers claim to serve others only to gain nearness to God, making explicit the rationale that the focus interrogates.
The verse asks whether those called besides God can remove or withhold harm and mercy, directly extending the utility test.
The Prophet rejects being commanded to worship other than God, restating the exclusive allegiance at stake.
The Prophet is forbidden to worship those called besides God and commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.
The challenge asks false objects to show what they created or what share they have in the heavens, testing their authority.
No one is further astray than one who calls on what cannot answer until the Day of Judgment.
When people are gathered, the called objects become enemies and deny the worship.
The named goddesses provide a direct example of the cult objects whose status Ibrahim's question refuses to assume.
The alleged deities are only names invented by people and their fathers without divine authority, directly joining false worship to inheritance.
Worship belongs to God alone, so no one is to be called alongside Him.
The idols have no feet, hands, eyes, or ears with which to act or respond, giving a detailed form of the focus passage's capability test.
They cannot hear a call to guidance or follow it, reinforcing the test of whether the worshipped objects hear.
Those who associated partners recognize them on the Day of Judgment, but the partners disown their association.
The calf neither returns speech nor controls harm or benefit, making the focus passage's test explicit within another idol narrative.
Calling another god alongside God is condemned as a claim without proof, directly rejecting unauthorized worship.
God asks the worshipped beings whether they led the servants astray, formally examining the claimed worship relationship.
The worshipped beings deny that it was fitting for them to be taken as protectors besides God.
The question whether God is better than the associates challenges the assumed parity of false worship.
God again asks where the alleged partners are, continuing the final exposure of their absence.
The command to show the alleged partners rejects their proposed equivalence with the Mighty and Wise God.
The aversion to God's exclusive mention and pleasure in mention of others reveals the divided allegiance that sustains idolatry.
Those taken as gods to bring nearness to God fail to help and disappear from their worshippers.
The rhetorical question whether there is a god besides God provides a concise monotheistic challenge to rival worship.
The command to preserve named idols shows inherited cult practice as an organized communal program.
